typical_mindset: The child understands how to generate the list of common factors or multiples, but starts counting one step too late — skipping the very first (smallest) common value and tacking on an extra one at the end instead, as if the list always had to have a fixed number of entries rather than starting from the true smallest common value.
explanation_strategy: Ask the child to go back to the very beginning and list multiples/factors of each number separately from the start, then point at the smallest value that appears in both lists, rather than being told 'you missed the first one.'

example_dialogue.text: Let's list the multiples of each number again, starting from the very first one. What's the smallest multiple of each number?
Oh, I started from the second one!
Good catch! What's the very first common one you see in both lists?

typical_mindset: A value that divides (or is a multiple of) only one of the two numbers is mistakenly included as if it were common to both — the check 'does this divide/multiply into BOTH numbers' isn't consistently applied to every candidate value.
explanation_strategy: Take the one extra value the child listed and ask them to check it against each of the two original numbers separately, one at a time, so they discover for themselves that it only works for one of them.

example_dialogue.text: Let's check that number against both of our original numbers, one at a time. Does it divide evenly into the first one?
Good. Now check the second number — does it divide evenly into that one too?

typical_mindset: The word 'common' isn't fully anchored to 'true of both numbers' — the child lists multiples or factors of just one of the two given numbers (usually the first one) and treats that whole list as if it already answers the question, without checking any value against the second number.
explanation_strategy: Ask the child to name both original numbers out loud before listing anything, then ask whose multiples/factors they were listing — theirs, or just one number's — so they notice for themselves that the second number was never used.

example_dialogue.text: We have two numbers here. Which ones did you list multiples for?
Just the first one, I think.
Right — for a COMMON multiple, we need it to show up in both numbers' lists. Let's list the second number's multiples too.

typical_mindset: LCM and HCF are both 'the special number you get from two numbers,' and which specific one a question wants isn't firmly tied to the words 'lowest common multiple' versus 'highest common factor' — the child correctly finds one of the two quantities but reports it even when the other one was asked for.
explanation_strategy: Before accepting the final number, ask the child to say in their own words whether the question wants the biggest number that divides into both, or the smallest number both divide into — then check which of their working numbers matches that description.

example_dialogue.text: Is this question asking for the biggest number that fits INTO both of ours, or the smallest number that BOTH of ours fit into?
The smallest one both fit into.
Right, that's the LCM. Which of the numbers you found matches that?
